rv.q: I'd give it a few more days before you go, but it's already the kind of show — clever, unpredictable new work with promise! — to which the city's theater should make haste to return.
Overall, the strong performances by Odom, Gonzalez-Cadel and Audrey Billings make the play worth seeing.

The result is like a Harold Pinter play filtered through the lens of our national fetish for instant gratification and individualism, with a dollop of late-capitalist assumptions about the value of human life.
Come ready to think and be prepared to leave wishing for more new works like this one: ingenious, thoughtful, and unafraid.
The performances are finely wrought, it’s staged with fleet and captivating brio, and the visual and design elements are all clean and sharp.
American Blues has a real treat in store for the adventurous theatergoer.
This is theatre that’s ferociously alive.
Acted with gonzo energy, directed with taut pacing and high intensity, “Things with Friends” works to some extent at the level of mood and theme.
Things With Friends makes a mistake at the beginning, then continues with that mistake for the entire 90 minutes.
This production with all of its parts is solid and entertaining and who could ask for anything more.

cn.t: This pitch-black climate comedy about a dystopian dinner party earns praise for sharp wit and strong performances, but critics are divided on its coherence, with some finding it bravely experimental and others calling it a confusing mess.
